name: Poverty Point
writeup: Between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, hunter-fisher-gatherers built six curved earthen ridges and several mounds here around a broad, flat plaza. Excavation and remote sensing show that rings of very large wooden posts once stood in that plaza. The Louisiana Division of Archaeology says no object clearly made only for ceremony has been found, the sources used here report no musical instruments, and nobody knows what was sung or danced. UNESCO describes the earthworks as made and used for residential and ceremonial purposes, and archaeologists suggest the plaza was a meeting place. That inference, not any surviving sound, is why the map's story of Louisiana gatherings begins at Poverty Point.
sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point <https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1435/> | 64 Parishes, Poverty Point <https://64parishes.org/entry/poverty-point> | Louisiana Office of Tourism, History and Artifacts of Poverty Point <https://www.povertypoint.us/history-artifacts-poverty-point> | Louisiana Division of Archaeology, Poverty Point: Ceremonial Life <https://www.crt.state.la.us/dataprojects/archaeology/povertypoint/ceremonial-life.html>

name: Marksville Prehistoric Indian Site
writeup: About 2,000 years ago people raised six mounds and a long semicircular earthen embankment here, a ceremonial center that gives the Marksville culture (about 1 to 400 CE) its name. The one burial mound held thirty-six people. At the related Crooks site, archaeologists found clusters of pebbles in graves that they interpret as the surviving contents of rattles whose casings rotted away, a rare physical hint of sound-making in ancient Louisiana. No such rattles are reported from Marksville itself, and the ceremonies held inside the embankment are inferred from the earthworks and burials. The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe now manages the site.
sources: 64 Parishes, Marksville Culture by Rebecca Saunders <https://64parishes.org/entry/marksville-culture> | Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, article on the Marksville site reposted from NOLA.com <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/this-archaeological-site-drew-pilgrims-2000-years-ago-now-there-are-big-plans-for-its-future/>

name: Adai Caddo Indian Nation Cultural Center
writeup: Northwest Louisiana is Caddo homeland, and Caddo music long predates the written record; 1500 is only a marker for that. Most Caddo people left Louisiana after 1835 and the Caddo Nation is now based in Oklahoma, where Drum Dance and Turkey Dance songs still recount tribal history and recall places such as Caddo Lake and the Ouachita River. The Adai Caddo Indian Nation, near Robeline, is a separate community, recognized as a tribe by the State of Louisiana. It keeps a cultural center and holds an annual powwow where members and visiting tribes from Texas and Oklahoma drum, sing and dance. In 2014 its chief described the old dances as prayers, for rain or for the safe return of warriors.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Caddo Homecoming by Dayna Bowker Lee (1998) <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/creole_art_caddo_homecomin.html> | WVUE Fox 8, Heart of Louisiana: The Adai Caddo Nation <https://www.fox8live.com/story/27421888/heart-of-louisiana-the-adai-caddo-nation/> | Natchitoches Convention and Visitors Bureau, Adai Indian Nation Cultural Center <https://explorenatchitoches.com/attractions/adai-indian-nation-cultural-center> | Adai Caddo Indian Nation, official site <https://www.adaicaddo.com/> | Louisiana Governor's Office of Indian Affairs, Federal and State Recognized Tribes <https://gov.louisiana.gov/federal-and-state-recognized-tribes>

name: Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana
writeup: The Chitimacha say they have always been here, and the tribe still lives on part of its homeland along Bayou Teche; 1500 only marks the edge of the written record. Visiting in January 1933, Frances Densmore heard from Benjamin Paul, Christine Paul and Delphine Decloux of a cane flute with four holes on top and one beneath, and of a dance tied to the chief's blessing of the seed corn. She also quoted John Swanton's 1911 account of a deerskin drum stretched over a clay pot and a dried alligator skin scraped with a stick. Densmore recorded no songs and judged the old ones lost. The tribe carries its culture forward through oral history, language revitalization and its museum.
sources: Frances Densmore, A Search for Songs among the Chitimacha Indians in Louisiana, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 133 (1943), full text <https://archive.org/stream/bulletin1331943smit/bulletin1331943smit_djvu.txt> | Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana, Tribal History <https://chitimacha.gov/history-culture/tribal-history> | Louisiana Office of Tourism, Chitimacha Museum <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/museums/chitimacha-museum>

name: Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana
writeup: The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe is the successor to the Tunica, Biloxi, Ofo and Avoyel peoples, whose songs are far older than any written account; 1500 is a placeholder for that deeper past. The Tunica moved down the Mississippi to the mouth of the Red River soon after French contact, and Marksville has been their main settlement since the 1780s. Today the tribe's Language and Culture Revitalization Program, based at the Cultural and Educational Resources Center, teaches the Tunica language through traditional songs and stories, and children learn traditional and powwow songs and dances. Each spring the tribe hosts a powwow on the reservation with intertribal dance competitions. Songs and stories passed down by community elders remain the core of this work.
sources: 64 Parishes, Tunica-Biloxi Tribe <https://64parishes.org/entry/tunica-biloxi-tribe> | Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, Language and Culture Revitalization Program <https://tunicabiloxi.org/tribal-info/departments/language-culture-revitalization-program> | Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, 26th Annual Pow Wow <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/tunica-biloxi-tribe-of-louisiana-celebrates-the-success-of-26th-annual-pow-wow-2/>

name: United Houma Nation
writeup: La Salle recorded a Houma village in 1682, and the Houma later moved south into the bayou country of Terrebonne and Lafourche, where most citizens live now. Their music is older than those records; 1500 simply marks the approach of the written record. Tribal leaders describe songs about the land, the water and past leaders, many of them prayer songs, sung in English, Choctaw and French and handed down by elders. Singers use hand drums and large hide drums, and a tribal member from Golden Meadow recalls that the Houma were traditionally stomp dancers with distinct ceremonial music. The nation gathers for an annual powwow. The point marks the tribe's main office on Monarch Drive in Houma.
sources: Garde Voir Ci (Nicholls State University), The Musical Backdrop <https://gardevoirci.nicholls.edu/2021/music/> | Garde Voir Ci (Nicholls State University), The Houma People <https://gardevoirci.nicholls.edu/2021/the-houma-people/> | United Houma Nation, About <https://unitedhoumanation.org/about/>

name: St. Louis Cathedral (colonial parish church)
writeup: European art music took root in Louisiana through the military and the Catholic Church, and this site was its center. Pierre Fleurtel was musician and schoolmaster for the St. Louis parish in 1725, joined the next year by François Saucier; the first parish church here was completed in 1727. That building burned in 1788, and its replacement was dedicated as a cathedral in 1794. Vicente Llorca, who served as church musician until 1803, is the first composer known to have worked in Louisiana. Little colonial music survives on paper, so much of what was sung here is known only from records of the people who made it.
sources: 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/?p=691> | 64 Parishes, St. Louis Cathedral <https://64parishes.org/?p=37591>

name: Congo Square
writeup: The 1724 Code Noir made Sunday a day without work for everyone in the colony, and enslaved Africans used it to gather, trade and make music in several places around the city. By the late 1740s this open ground behind the town was one of them, serving as a market and meeting place through the French and Spanish periods. An 1817 ordinance then confined such gatherings to this square, where hundreds danced the Bamboula, Calinda and Congo to gourd rattles and instruments modelled on African ones. The detailed eyewitness accounts date from after 1803; the colonial-era gatherings are documented more thinly. The start year is approximate.
sources: 64 Parishes, Congo Square <https://64parishes.org/entry/congo-square> | The Cultural Landscape Foundation, Congo Square <https://www.tclf.org/landscapes/congo-square> | New Orleans Historical, Congo Square: Mythology and Music <https://neworleanshistorical.org/items/show/745>

name: Old Ursuline Convent
writeup: The Ursuline nuns reached New Orleans in 1727 and made music part of the schooling they gave girls. In 1754 a donor known only as Monsieur Nicollet sent them a bound manuscript, copied in 1736 by a scribe signing C. D., of 294 sacred songs that fit new devotional words to tunes by Lully, Couperin, Campra, Clérambault and others. It is the oldest known music manuscript in Louisiana and stayed with the Ursulines until The Historic New Orleans Collection acquired their archives in 1998. The convent on Chartres Street, finished in the early 1750s, is the building most closely tied to the book's arrival.
listen_1_label: Songs from the Ursuline manuscript performed by Le Concert Lorrain (The Historic New Orleans Collection)
sources: The Historic New Orleans Collection, Ursuline Music Manuscript <https://hnoc.org/research-collections/collection-highlights/ursuline-music-manuscript> | 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/?p=691> | Wikipedia, Old Ursuline Convent, New Orleans (building dates only) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Ursuline_Convent,_New_Orleans>

name: Acadian arrival at the Attakapas (Acadian Memorial)
writeup: In 1765, ten years after their deportation from Nova Scotia, Acadian exiles began reaching Louisiana, and 193 of them were sent to the Attakapas district, spreading out along the waterways around what became St. Martinville. No one wrote down what they sang that year. Folklorists do report that unaccompanied ballads were among the earliest music in French Louisiana, that Acadian families held on to theirs for generations, and that the fiddle was the first instrument in common use. From that stock of western French song, mixed over the following century with Native, African, Spanish and Anglo-American music, Cajun music grew. The Acadian Memorial stands beside Bayou Teche.
sources: City of St. Martinville, Our History <https://stmartinville.gov/our-history> | Barry Jean Ancelet, Cajun Music: A Louisiana French Tradition, Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife program book (1983) <https://folklife-media.si.edu/docs/festival/program-book-articles/FESTBK1983_15.pdf> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Cajun Music: Alive and Well in Louisiana by Ann Savoy (1990) <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/creole_art_cajunmusic_aliv.html>

name: Los Isleños Museum Complex
writeup: Between 1778 and 1783 about 2,000 Canary Islanders came to Spanish Louisiana under Governor Bernardo de Gálvez. Of their four settlements, only the one in St. Bernard kept its Spanish identity, and later fishing villages such as Delacroix grew from it. The Isleños sang décimas, a Spanish form traceable to the fifteenth century, which here became sung stories about neighbours, scandals, tall tales and daily events. Irván Pérez, the best-known singer, received a National Heritage Fellowship in 1991 and died in 2008. The museum complex in St. Bernard interprets this heritage and hosts the annual Fiesta de los Isleños.
listen_1_label: La Décima de Wila, sung by Irván Pérez, 1988 (64 Parishes, Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities)
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, The Evolution of the Isleño Identity by Sara-Ann Harris <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/islenos.html> | Louisiana Office of Tourism, Los Isleños Museum <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/museums/los-islenos-museum> | 64 Parishes, La Décima de Wila (audio) <https://64parishes.org/entry-audio/la-decima-de-wila>

name: Théâtre St. Pierre (site)
writeup: New Orleans's first French-language theatre opened in October 1792, under Spanish rule, on St. Peter Street between Royal and Bourbon. On May 22, 1796 it staged André Grétry's Sylvain, the first opera known to have been performed in the city, which began an operatic tradition that New Orleans kept up almost without a break. The composer Joseph Arquier worked in the city from 1800 to 1803. The building is long gone and the point marks the block where it stood, not a surviving structure. Sources differ on the end: 64 Parishes says the theatre closed in 1803, while another account has it shut that year for repairs, reopened in 1804 and finally auctioned off in 1810.
sources: 64 Parishes, Opera and Ballet <https://64parishes.org/entry/opera-and-ballet> | 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/?p=691> | Wikipedia, Theatre de la Rue Saint Pierre (used for the 1810 date and block location) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_de_la_Rue_Saint_Pierre>

name: Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana
writeup: The Koasati, or Coushatta, had migrated into Louisiana by 1795 and acquired their present lands near Elton in 1884; their song and dance traditions are much older than that move. The tribe describes the Stomp Dance as danced counter-clockwise around a fire at night, with men calling the songs and setting the pace and women keeping rhythm with turtle shakers, the smoke carrying prayers upward. The tribe notes that few members now know the original dances and songs, and it is working to pass them on. Dances such as the Round Dance and the Swan Dance are performed today, and the tribe hosts a large annual powwow.
listen_1_label: Coushatta Round Dance and Swan Dance videos (National Park Service, Jean Lafitte NHP)
sources: Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Coushatta Powwow <https://coushattapowwow.com/> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Keeping It Alive: Koasati Crafts and Storytelling <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Virtual_Books/Keeping_It/creole_book_keep_koas.html> | National Park Service, Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana <https://www.nps.gov/jela/learn/coushatta-tribe-of-louisiana.htm>

name: Théâtre d'Orléans
writeup: Opened in 1815 on Orleans Street between Royal and Bourbon, then rebuilt after a fire under manager John Davis, a refugee from Saint-Domingue, the Théâtre d'Orléans made New Orleans the leading American city for French opera. Davis recruited singers and players directly from France, staged the American debuts of four Rossini operas between 1828 and 1833, and took his company on summer tours of the Northeast. From 1841 to 1860 the house gave 1,550 performances of 109 operas by 35 composers. The theater burned in 1866. Its adjoining ballroom survived and is now part of the Bourbon Orleans Hotel.
sources: 64 Parishes, Orleans Theatre <https://64parishes.org/entry/orleans-theatre> | 64 Parishes, Opera and Ballet <https://64parishes.org/entry/opera-and-ballet> | Wikipedia, Théâtre d'Orléans (1866 fire, ballroom, coordinates) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_d%27Orl%C3%A9ans>

name: Perseverance Hall No. 4
writeup: Built in 1819 and 1820 for a Masonic lodge chartered by refugees from Saint-Domingue, this is the oldest Masonic temple in Louisiana. The lodge rented its ground floor for public events to bring in income, and held its rites and dances upstairs. In the early 1900s those dances featured the first jazz bands; Sidney Bechet played here as a boy, and riverboat captain Verne Streckfus came to scout Black musicians for his excursion steamers. Saved from demolition during urban renewal in the early 1970s, the hall now stands inside Louis Armstrong Park as the centerpiece of New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park.
sources: A Closer Walk, Perseverance Masonic Lodge No. 4 <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/perseverance-masonic-lodge-no-4/> | Wikipedia, New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Jazz_National_Historical_Park>

name: Milneburg
writeup: Milneburg grew up where the Pontchartrain Railroad, running from 1831, met the lake. A boardwalk ran out over the water to a pier and lighthouse, lined with dance pavilions and rented stilt houses called camps. By the early 1900s there was music nearly every day and most of all on weekends, when bands from all over the city, Black and white, listened to and tried to outdo one another at Quarrella's Pavilion and camps such as the Owl Club and the Little Brown Jug. Cornetist Sharkey Bonano grew up here, and the jazz standard Milenberg Joys carries the name. Seawall and landfill work after 1927 erased the resort.
listen_1_label: Emile Barnes, Milenberg Joys (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: 64 Parishes, Jazz at the Lakefront, by Bruce Boyd Raeburn <https://64parishes.org/jazz-at-the-lakefront> | National Park Service, Jazz Neighborhoods Map <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz-map.htm> | Wikipedia, Milneburg <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milneburg>

name: First Presbyterian Church, Lafayette Square (site)
writeup: The Presbyterian church built in 1835 on the upriver side of Lafayette Square served the English-speaking Protestants of the American sector, and Warren Kimball's research shows how much of their music passed through it. Its choir was known as one of the best in the city. A sacred concert here in 1841 raised money for the temperance society. On July 1, 1842, the new public schools of the Second Municipality held an exhibition here at which Frederick Müller, lately of Boston, led the children's singing, and that November he opened a singing school in the basement. It burned in 1854. Its Gothic successor of 1857 housed a Henry Erben organ and was demolished in 1938 for a federal building.
sources: Warren Keith Kimball, Northern Music Culture in Antebellum New Orleans (PhD diss., Louisiana State University, 2017), chs. 2-4 <https://repository.lsu.edu/gradschool_dissertations/4119> | Richard Campanella, New Orleans' Third First Presbyterian Church, Preservation in Print (May 2015) <https://richcampanella.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/article_Campanella_Preservation-in-Print_2015_June_First-PresbyterianChurch.pdf>

name: St. Charles Theatre (site)
writeup: James Caldwell, who had opened the English-language Camp Street Theatre in 1824, built the St. Charles Theatre for the audiences of the American sector. It opened on November 30, 1835, with 4,100 seats, and was counted among the finest houses in the country until fire destroyed it in March 1842. A replacement opened the next year. There, in February and March 1851, Jenny Lind sang thirteen sold-out concerts; the avenue was made one-way on concert nights, and William Mayo's Camp Street shop published a mazurka in her honor. That building burned in 1899. A third theatre on the lot, for a time the Orpheum, closed in 1965 and was razed. The point marks the site at 426 St. Charles Avenue.

name: Rev. Theodore Clapp's church and the New Orleans Sacred Music Society (site)
writeup: Theodore Clapp's Congregational, later Unitarian, church at St. Charles and Gravier streets was the first home of oratorio in New Orleans. In February 1836 The Bee announced a grand oratorio here with Handel's Messiah and Haydn's Creation on the bill. In 1842 amateurs from the city's American population founded the New Orleans Sacred Music Society, which its conductor Frederick Müller likened to Boston's Handel and Haydn Society. Its first public concert was given here on May 18, 1842, and it later sang The Creation here complete, announced as a first for the city. The society was still meeting in the church in 1850. The building burned in 1851; the point marks the street corner, not a surviving structure.

name: Mayo and Werlein music store, No. 5 Camp Street (site)
writeup: Sheet music tied antebellum New Orleans to the Northern trade, and its busiest counter was 5 Camp Street. William T. Mayo bought Emile Johns's Chartres Street music business and moved it into the American sector; Warren Kimball dates the purchase to 1841, most other accounts to 1846. Mayo issued pieces jointly with New York's William Hall & Son, sold pianos and concert tickets and advertised almost daily. Philip Werlein, a Bavarian-born music teacher, took over in the early 1850s. In 1860 he issued the first Southern edition of Dixie, at first without crediting Dan Emmett, and in 1862 he closed the store under Union occupation. The point marks the Canal Street end of Camp Street; the exact lot is unconfirmed.

name: St. Augustine Church, Tremé
writeup: Free people of color founded this parish in 1841 on land that had been part of the Claude Tremé plantation, and the church was dedicated the following year. It is regarded as the oldest Black Catholic parish in the United States. Its founders bought pews along the side aisles so that enslaved people could worship there too. The church sits at the heart of the neighborhood that produced generations of brass band and jazz players: clarinetist Sidney Bechet worshipped here, as did Mardi Gras Indian chief Tootie Montana. The parish still holds gospel jazz Masses, and its Tomb of the Unknown Slave was dedicated in 2004.
sources: New Orleans Historical, St. Augustine Catholic Church <https://neworleanshistorical.org/items/show/551> | Wikipedia, St. Augustine Church (New Orleans) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Augustine_Church_(New_Orleans)>

name: Economy Hall
writeup: The Société d'Economie et d'Assistance Mutuelle, a mutual aid society formed by free people of color in 1836, opened its hall on Ursulines Avenue in Tremé in 1857 with an evening of orchestral waltzes. By 1875 the society was parading with brass bands, and around 1900 its dance floor became one of the first homes of jazz. Buddy Bolden played here; Kid Ory rented the hall on Monday nights from 1912, and a young Louis Armstrong worked in his band. Bassist Pops Foster said that a musician who made Economy Hall had made it to the top. The society sold the building in 1945, and Hurricane Betsy wrecked it in 1965.
listen_1_label: The Eureka Brass Band, The Music of New Orleans, Vol. 2 (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: A Closer Walk, Economy Hall <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/economy-hall/> | The Historic New Orleans Collection, First Draft, on Economy Hall <https://hnoc.org/publishing/first-draft/what-do-you-know-about-economy-hall-jazz-fest-tents-namesake-was-once-> | National Park Service, Jazz Neighborhoods Map <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz-map.htm>

name: French Opera House
writeup: When a dispute at the aging Théâtre d'Orléans pushed its impresario to build a new house, the French Opera House opened at 541 Bourbon Street on December 1, 1859, with Rossini's Guillaume Tell. For sixty years it was the social center of the French Quarter, home to opera, plays, dances and Carnival balls, and the stage for the Metropolitan Opera's first New Orleans visit in 1901. By the mid-1870s people of color were confined to an upper gallery. Jelly Roll Morton remembered going as a young man and said it helped set him on his path. Fire destroyed the building in December 1919; a hotel now stands on the site.
sources: A Closer Walk, French Opera House <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/french-opera-house/> | 64 Parishes, Opera and Ballet <https://64parishes.org/entry/opera-and-ballet>

name: Kid Ory's birthplace, Woodland Plantation
writeup: Trombonist Edward "Kid" Ory was born on Christmas Day 1886 on Woodland Plantation, a sugar estate whose 1793 house was also the starting point of the 1811 German Coast uprising of enslaved people. As a boy he played fish fries on homemade instruments, then formed the Woodland Band and took it to New Orleans around 1910, where he hired Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong and pioneered the tailgate style of jazz trombone. In 1944 he recorded the first documented jazz song sung in Louisiana Creole. The house, listed on the National Register, operated as a museum honoring Ory in 2021 and 2022 and now belongs to a nonprofit, the Descendants Project.
listen_1_label: Ory's Sunshine Orchestra, Ory's Creole Trombone (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: 64 Parishes, Kid Ory <https://64parishes.org/entry/kid-ory> | The Cultural Landscape Foundation, Woodland Plantation <https://tclf.org/woodland-plantation> | Wikipedia, 1811 Kid Ory Historic House <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1811_Kid_Ory_Historic_House>

name: True Friends Benevolent Hall
writeup: The True Friends Benevolent Association, a Black mutual aid society that covered its members' medical and burial costs, built this hall on Lessard Street in the 1880s. It hosted Carnival balls, dances, plays and jam sessions in a river town full of musicians. The best known was violinist and bandleader Claiborne Williams (1868-1952), who grew up on a plantation, made his first violin from a cigar box, toured as far as Europe and taught many local players. A jazz plaza close by also honors parish natives King Oliver and Pops Foster. Later a Chitlin' Circuit stop for Fats Domino and James Brown, the hall closed in the 1980s and is being restored by the River Road African American Museum.
sources: Historical Marker Database, African American Life marker, Donaldsonville <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=155974> | Country Roads Magazine, True Friends Benevolent Hall <https://countryroadsmagazine.com/art-and-culture/people-places/rraam-true-friends-benevolent-hall/> | KALB, Historic True Friends Hall restoration project <https://www.kalb.com/2026/01/06/historic-true-friends-hall-restoration-project-aims-preserve-louisianas-musical-heritage> | Read the Plaque, Bicentennial Jazz Plaza <https://readtheplaque.com/plaque/bicentennial-jazz-plaza>

name: Jelly Roll Morton's childhood home
writeup: Ferdinand "Jelly Roll" Morton grew up in this Creole cottage at 1443 Frenchmen Street, in a French-speaking, educated Catholic Creole family. His birth year is given as either 1885 or 1890. His relatives respected the musicians of the French Opera House and little else in the trade, so the teenage pianist took his talent to the parlors of Storyville and then on the road. He became one of the greatest pianists, composers and arrangers of early jazz, blending classical training, blues and the Caribbean rhythms he called the Spanish tinge in pieces such as King Porter Stomp. The house survives; it was renovated after Hurricane Katrina and rented to musicians.
listen_1_label: Jelly Roll Morton, Piano Classics 1923-24 (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: A Closer Walk, Jelly Roll Morton's House <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/jelly-roll-mortons-house/> | 64 Parishes, Jelly Roll Morton <https://64parishes.org/entry/jelly-roll-morton>

name: Dew Drop Social and Benevolent Hall
writeup: Black residents of Mandeville organized the Dew Drop Social and Benevolent Association in 1885 to look after neighbors who were shut out of health care, loans and other services, and in 1895 they built this plain wooden hall on Lamarque Street to meet in and to raise money with dances. New Orleans musicians crossed Lake Pontchartrain by steamboat to play them; Kid Ory, Buddy Petit and a young Louis Armstrong all performed here. Hardly changed since it was built, it is described as the oldest unaltered rural jazz hall anywhere. The City of Mandeville and the Friends of the Dew Drop now present concerts in it each spring and fall.

name: Eagle Saloon and Odd Fellows and Masonic Hall
writeup: Two joined buildings at South Rampart and Perdido streets formed one of the first regular homes of jazz. The Odd Fellows and Masonic Hall was established in 1897, with a third-floor ballroom for dances; the Eagle Saloon opened next door in 1908 and became a gathering place for musicians. Buddy Bolden, John Robichaux, Frankie Dusen, Sidney Bechet, Bunk Johnson, King Oliver, Freddie Keppard and Baby Dodds are all tied to the site, and brass band parades set out from the door. The saloon building at 401 South Rampart survives, long vacant.
listen_1_label: Baby Dodds, Footnotes to Jazz, Vol. 1: Talking and Drum Solos (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: A Closer Walk, Eagle Saloon / Odd Fellows and Masonic Hall <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/eagle-saloon/> | National Park Service, Jazz Neighborhoods Map <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz-map.htm>

name: Storyville
writeup: From 1897 to 1917 the blocks behind the French Quarter along Basin Street were the city's legal red-light district, nicknamed for Sidney Story, the alderman who wrote the ordinance. Its parlors, saloons and dance halls gave steady work to musicians: Jelly Roll Morton played piano in the brothels as a teenager, and Kid Ory, King Oliver and Louis Armstrong all worked in the District, where Pete Lala's saloon was a leading music room. Jazz was not born here, as legend claims, but the District carried the new music to a wider audience. Closed under wartime pressure from the Navy in 1917, it was mostly cleared for the Iberville housing project by 1940.
listen_1_label: The Music of New Orleans, Vol. 4: The Birth of Jazz, including Storyville and Tom Anderson's (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: A Closer Walk, Storyville <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/storyville/> | National Park Service, Jazz Neighborhoods Map <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz-map.htm> | 64 Parishes, Jelly Roll Morton <https://64parishes.org/entry/jelly-roll-morton>

name: Union Sons Hall (Funky Butt Hall)
writeup: Union Sons Hall, at 1319 Perdido Street, was one of the busiest dance halls in the Black back-of-town district that the whites-only Storyville excluded. Around 1900 its biggest draw was cornetist Buddy Bolden, whose loud, bluesy, improvised playing is the earliest documented New Orleans jazz. His band played late into the night and cleared out in time for the First Lincoln Baptist Church to hold Sunday services in the same room. The nickname comes from the Bolden tune also known as Buddy Bolden's Blues. Louis Armstrong, who grew up nearby, remembered hearing Bolden here. The building was torn down in the mid-1950s, when the block was cleared for the present City Hall.
listen_1_label: The Music of New Orleans, Vol. 4: The Birth of Jazz, with recollections of Buddy Bolden (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: A Closer Walk, Union Sons Hall (aka Funky Butt Hall) <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/union-sons-hall-aka-funky-butt-hall/> | Verite News, Funky Butt Hall: Where Louis Armstrong heard Buddy Bolden play <https://veritenews.org/2024/07/01/bitd-funky-butt-hall-louis-armstrong-buddy-bolden/> | 64 Parishes, Buddy Bolden <https://64parishes.org/entry/buddy-bolden>

name: Louis Armstrong's birthplace, Jane Alley
writeup: Louis Armstrong was born on August 4, 1901, in a small wooden house on Jane Alley, in a back-of-town neighborhood rough enough to be called the Battlefield. He liked to give his birthday as July 4, 1900. He later moved to Perdido Street near Funky Butt Hall and the dance halls of South Rampart Street, where he heard the first generation of jazz players and earned money for his first cornet working for the Karnofsky family. The birthplace was demolished in 1964 to clear ground for the city's traffic court and police headquarters on South Broad Street; a marker in the plaza identifies the site.
listen_1_label: Louis Armstrong House Museum, biography timeline with audio of Armstrong
sources: A Closer Walk, Louis Armstrong's Birthplace <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/louis-armstrongs-birthplace/> | Louis Armstrong House Museum, Biography <https://www.louisarmstronghouse.org/biography>

name: Lincoln Park and Johnson Park
writeup: The Standard Brewing Company opened Lincoln Park in May 1902 as an amusement ground for Black New Orleanians, with a skating rink, balloon ascensions, prizefights and vaudeville for fifteen cents. Johnson Park occupied the next block for several years. The two became famous for Sunday band battles around 1905 between Buddy Bolden's rough uptown band and John Robichaux's polished downtown orchestra. Jelly Roll Morton recalled that when the crowd was thin Bolden would point his cornet toward town and blow to call people in. Bunk Johnson and Freddie Keppard were also heard here. Lincoln Park lasted until 1930, and both blocks along South Carrollton Avenue have since been redeveloped.
sources: A Closer Walk, Lincoln and Johnson Parks <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/lincoln-johnson-parks/> | Wikipedia, Lincoln Park (New Orleans) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Park_(New_Orleans)> | National Park Service, Jazz Neighborhoods Map <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz-map.htm>

name: St. Paul's Bottoms and Fannin Street
writeup: In 1903 Shreveport set aside a neighborhood known as St. Paul's Bottoms, bounded on the south by Fannin Street, as a legal red-light district. For fourteen years Fannin Street was a row of saloons, dance halls and brothels, among them the Octoroon Club. Huddie Ledbetter, the Caddo Parish farm boy later known as Lead Belly, began performing here as a young man, and the mix of styles he heard along the street shaped his playing. He told the story in his song Fannin Street. Voters closed the district in 1917. The area was later renamed Ledbetter Heights in his honor, and its surviving buildings are listed on the National Register.
listen_1_label: Lead Belly, Fannin Street (Mister Tom Hughes Town) (Smithsonian Folkways)
listen_2_label: Lead Belly: The Smithsonian Folkways Collection
sources: 64 Parishes, St. Paul's Bottoms <https://64parishes.org/?p=56889> | National Park Service, Huddie William Leadbelly Ledbetter <https://www.nps.gov/locations/lowermsdeltaregion/leadbelly.htm> | 64 Parishes, Huddie Lead Belly Ledbetter <https://64parishes.org/entry/lead-belly>

name: Colored Waifs' Home for Boys
writeup: Opened in 1906 by Captain Joseph Jones so that Black boys in trouble with the law would not be locked up with adults, this reform school on City Park Avenue was run like a military post. Louis Armstrong was sent here after firing a pistol in the street on New Year's Eve 1912. Over the next eighteen months music instructor Peter Davis taught him bugle and cornet, and Armstrong rose to lead the Home's brass band, which marched at public events around the city. He left in June 1914 a working musician. The Home merged with the Milne Boys Home in 1932, and the old building was later torn down.
sources: A Closer Walk, Colored Waifs Home for Boys <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/colored-waifs-home-boys/> | Verite News, Colored Waif's Home founded to keep Black boys out of Parish Prison <https://veritenews.org/2024/06/12/bitd-colored-waifs-home-parish-prison/> | Louis Armstrong House Museum, Biography <https://www.louisarmstronghouse.org/biography>

name: Iroquois Theater
writeup: The Iroquois opened in 1912 at 413 South Rampart Street as a vaudeville and picture house, and it was among the first theaters anywhere to present jazz and blues as a show to sit and listen to. A house band accompanied silent films and touring acts such as headliner Butler "String Beans" May; pianist Clarence Williams and guitarist Lonnie Johnson performed here, and a young Louis Armstrong won a talent contest on its stage. Live shows ended about 1920 and the building carried on as a movie theater. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, it still stands on a block crowded with early jazz landmarks.
listen_1_label: Lonnie Johnson, Careless Love (Smithsonian Folkways)
sources: A Closer Walk, Iroquois Theater <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/iroquois-theater/> | National Park Service, Jazz Neighborhoods Map <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz-map.htm>

name: Calanthean Temple
writeup: The Grand Court Order of Calanthe, a Black women's fraternal organization led by Cora Murdock Allen, completed this four-story building on Texas Avenue in 1923. It held offices for Black doctors, dentists and lawyers, and its rooftop garden became a leading dance spot for African Americans in Jim Crow Shreveport. Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, Jelly Roll Morton, Cab Calloway and Louis Jordan are among those reported to have played there, and touring musicians came up for late jam sessions after their engagements at segregated venues. The roof garden's heyday was the 1930s and 1940s. The long-neglected building is now part of the Shreveport Common revitalization effort.
sources: 64 Parishes: Music in the Court of Calanthe <https://64parishes.org/music-in-the-court-of-calanthe> | Downtown Shreveport: Calanthean Temple, rooftop dances and legendary musicians <https://downtownshreveport.com/featured/calanthean-temple-rooftop-dances-and-legendary-musicians/>

name: Slim Harpo Marker and Mulatto Bend Cemetery
writeup: James Moore, who recorded as Slim Harpo, was born in February 1924 at Lobdell in West Baton Rouge Parish. He worked as a longshoreman and construction laborer and played Baton Rouge bars before his recording career began in 1957 with "I'm a King Bee." "Rainin' in My Heart" (1961) and "Baby Scratch My Back" (1966) both reached the top five of the rhythm and blues chart, and the Rolling Stones, the Kinks and many others recorded his songs. He died of a heart attack in January 1970, aged 45 (the marker says 46), and is buried beside his parents in Mulatto Bend Cemetery. A state historical marker stands at U.S. 190 and South Mulatto Bend Road.
sources: West Baton Rouge Parish: James Slim Harpo Moore <https://wbrparish.org/277/James-Slim-Harpo-Moore> | Historical Marker Database: James Slim Harpo Moore <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=85007>

name: Temple Roof Garden (Prince Hall Masonic Temple)
writeup: Built in 1924 for the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows, the four-story building at 1335 North Boulevard held the Temple Theatre and, on its top floor, a ballroom called the Temple Roof Garden. With no comparable hall open to them, Black Baton Rougeans and students from Southern University danced here to touring bands; people interviewed for the building's National Register nomination recalled Fats Waller, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong and Cab Calloway. A 1938 advertisement called it the finest dancing hall in the South. The Prince Hall Masons bought the building in 1948, and it was listed on the National Register in 1994.
sources: National Park Service: National Register nomination, Prince Hall Masonic Temple <https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/fd7b1aff-b4b7-4a71-b1e2-91b01cdcb059> | Wikipedia: Prince Hall Masonic Temple (Baton Rouge, Louisiana) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Hall_Masonic_Temple_(Baton_Rouge,_Louisiana)>

name: Amédé Ardoin Statue (St. Landry Parish Visitor Center)
writeup: Amédé Ardoin, a Creole accordionist and singer from the Eunice and Basile area, was one of the first Creole musicians to make records. Between 1929 and 1934 he cut 34 songs, some with the Cajun fiddler Dennis McGee, and their waltzes and two-steps became a foundation for both Cajun music and zydeco; Iry LeJeune and Clifton Chenier drew on them. After a beating from which he never recovered, Ardoin died in 1942 in the state hospital at Pineville and was buried in an unmarked grave. On March 11, 2018, this steel statue by Russell Whiting, showing him standing on his accordion with a lemon in his hand, was unveiled to bring him home symbolically.
listen_1_label: Amédé Ardoin, I'm Never Comin' Back (Smithsonian Folkways / Arhoolie)
sources: 64 Parishes: Amédé Ardoin <https://64parishes.org/entry/amede-ardoin> | St. Landry Parish Tourist Commission: Amédé Ardoin Statue <https://cajuntravel.com/things/amede-ardoin-statue/> | KLFY: Life-sized statue honoring slain musician Amédé Ardoin unveiled <https://www.klfy.com/local/life-sized-statue-honoring-slain-musician-amede-ardoin-unveiled-sunday-in-st-landry-parish/> | Smithsonian Folkways: I'm Never Comin' Back <https://folkways.si.edu/amede-ardoin/im-never-comin-back/cajun-zydeco/music/album/smithsonian>

name: Miller-Roy Building and Savoy Ballroom
writeup: Two Black physicians, J.T. Miller and J.C. Roy, built this three-story block at DeSiard and Tenth streets in 1929 as a home for African American business in segregated Monroe. Offices, a pharmacy and a newspaper filled the lower floors, and the third floor was the Savoy Ballroom, a Chitlin' Circuit stop that brought Louis Armstrong, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and later Otis Redding and Percy Sledge to northeast Louisiana. The building was eventually condemned and approved for demolition, but it was listed on the National Register in 2011 and has since been renovated as apartments with community space.
sources: 64 Parishes: Monroe's Miller-Roy Building <https://64parishes.org/monroes-miller-roy-building>

name: Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola
writeup: In the summer of 1933 folklorist John Lomax and his son Alan brought a recording machine to the state prison farm at Angola, collecting African American songs for the Library of Congress. The warden pointed them to a prisoner named Huddie Ledbetter, known as Lead Belly. They returned in July 1934 with better equipment and recorded him again, including "Irene," the song later famous as "Goodnight Irene," "The Midnight Special," and a plea addressed to Governor O.K. Allen. Lead Belly was released that August and went on to national fame. The sessions made Angola a landmark in the documentation of American folk music.
listen_1_label: Angola Prisoners' Blues (Smithsonian Folkways / Arhoolie)
sources: 64 Parishes: Lead Belly <https://64parishes.org/entry/lead-belly> | National Endowment for the Humanities: Come Prepared to Travel, Bring Guitar <https://www.neh.gov/article/come-prepared-travel-bring-guitar> | Wikipedia: Louisiana State Penitentiary <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_State_Penitentiary>

name: Blue Room, Roosevelt Hotel
writeup: The Blue Room opened in the Roosevelt Hotel in 1935 and for decades was the city's premier supper club. Touring big bands led by Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey and Guy Lombardo played here, followed by singers such as Lena Horne, Sarah Vaughan, Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. Radio station WWL carried live broadcasts of the dance bands, so the room's sound reached listeners far beyond the hotel. It stopped operating as a supper club in 1989, closed after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and returned when the restored Roosevelt reopened in 2009.
sources: New Orleans Magazine: Feeling Blue (Seale Paterson, 2009) <https://www.myneworleans.com/feeling-blue/> | Wikipedia: The Roosevelt New Orleans <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Roosevelt_New_Orleans>

name: Buddy Guy Birthplace
writeup: George "Buddy" Guy was born on July 30, 1936, in Lettsworth, a rural community in northern Pointe Coupee Parish, the son of a sharecropper. He absorbed the sounds of Louisiana players and of Mississippi bluesmen such as Muddy Waters and B.B. King, and in 1957 left Baton Rouge for Chicago, where he became a giant of electric blues guitar. A Mississippi Blues Trail marker was unveiled on December 8, 2018, beside Louisiana Highway 418 at Sharkles Place; its text says the family's house stood a short distance away. The highway through Lettsworth is now named Buddy Guy Way.
sources: OffBeat Magazine: Buddy Guy Mississippi Blues Trail marker <https://offbeat.com/news/buddy-guy-mississippi-blues-trail> | Historical Marker Database: Buddy Guy <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=127700>

name: Dew Drop Inn
writeup: Barber Frank Painia opened the Dew Drop Inn at 2836 LaSalle Street in 1939 and added a nightclub in 1945. In segregated New Orleans it gave Black entertainers both a stage and a respectable place to sleep. Its floor shows drew Ray Charles, Big Joe Turner, Guitar Slim, Earl King, Allen Toussaint, Dave Bartholomew and James Booker, and Little Richard sang about the place. The music room went quiet around 1970 and Painia died in 1972. After decades of decline the building was restored and reopened in 2024 as a hotel and music venue.
sources: 64 Parishes: Dew Drop Inn <https://64parishes.org/entry/dew-drop-inn> | Wikipedia: Dew Drop Inn (New Orleans, Louisiana) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dew_Drop_Inn_(New_Orleans,_Louisiana)>

name: Haney's Big House
writeup: William Haney, a World War I veteran and Black businessman, turned a 1930s barbecue stand in Ferriday into Haney's Big House, a nightclub with a dance floor, a motel for performers and even a bus ticket counter. At its peak from 1940 to 1966 it was a stop on the Chitlin' Circuit, hosting Ray Charles, B.B. King, Big Joe Turner, Roy Brown and Irma Thomas. A young Jerry Lee Lewis and his cousin Jimmy Swaggart listened from the sidewalk, then tried the music at the piano. The club burned in 1966 and was not rebuilt. A town historical marker at North First and Greathouse streets, mapped here, tells the story.
sources: 64 Parishes: William Haney and Haney's Big House <https://64parishes.org/entry/william-haney-and-haneys-big-house> | Explore Louisiana: Haney's Big House <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/music/haneys-big-house> | Historical Marker Database: Haney's Big House <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=119690>

name: Goldband Records
writeup: Eddie Shuler, a Texas-born guitarist who came to Lake Charles in the early 1940s, started Goldband in 1945 to record his own band and soon turned to the musicians around him. The complex on Church Street held a studio, production rooms and a record shop. Its catalog ran from Iry LeJeune's Cajun accordion to Boozoo Chavis's "Paper in My Shoe" (1954), Phil Phillips's swamp pop hit "Sea of Love" (1959) and the first record by a thirteen-year-old Dolly Parton. When Shuler died in 2005 Goldband was described as the country's longest-established independent label. The complex was demolished in 2017; a historical marker stands on Church Street.
sources: 64 Parishes: Goldband Records <https://64parishes.org/entry/goldband-records> | Read the Plaque: Goldband Studios <https://readtheplaque.com/plaque/goldband-studios> | Historical Marker Database: Goldband Studio <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=116634>

name: J&M Recording Studio
writeup: Cosimo Matassa was still a teenager when he put recording gear in a back room of his family's J&M Music Shop at North Rampart and Dumaine streets. The room measured about fifteen by sixteen feet, yet from the mid-1940s until Matassa moved to Governor Nicholls Street in 1956 it captured the sound that became rock and roll: Roy Brown's "Good Rocking Tonight" (1947), Fats Domino's "The Fat Man" (1949), Professor Longhair's "Tipitina" (1953) and Little Richard's "Tutti Frutti" (1955). The building, long a laundromat, still stands on the edge of the French Quarter.
sources: 64 Parishes: Cosimo Matassa <https://64parishes.org/entry/cosimo-matassa> | A Closer Walk: J&M Recording Studio <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/jm-recording-studio/> | Historical Marker Database: First Recording Studio of Cosimo Matassa <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=149066>

name: Fred's Lounge
writeup: Alfred "Fred" Tate bought a bar on Mamou's Sixth Street on November 20, 1946, and it became a small-town headquarters for the Cajun revival. Tate helped bring back Mamou's Courir de Mardi Gras, and in the 1960s his friend Revon Reed began broadcasting Cajun music from the lounge on Saturday mornings in Louisiana French; accounts date the show to 1962 or to 1968. It still airs, now over KVPI in Ville Platte. After Fred died in 1992, his former wife Sue Vasseur, known as Tante Sue, remained the lounge's hostess until her death in 2025. Fred's opens on Saturday mornings, with a Cajun band and dancing from nine o'clock.
sources: Lafayette Travel: Fred's in Mamou <https://lafayettetravel.com/motorcycle/freds-in-mamou> | Evangeline Today: Taunt Sue de Mamou dies (2025) <https://www.evangelinetoday.com/news-local/taunt-sue-de-mamou-dies> | Wikipedia: Fred's Lounge <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred%27s_Lounge>

name: J.D. Miller Recording Studio (museum at Crowley City Hall)
writeup: J.D. Miller began recording Cajun bands in 1946 and set up a simple studio in Crowley in 1947, first at home and then at his M&S Electric shop on North Parkerson Avenue. He went on to record nearly every south Louisiana style: Cajun, country, zydeco, swamp pop and, above all, the swamp blues of Lightnin' Slim and Slim Harpo, which he licensed to Excello Records. The legacy is mixed, since in the 1960s Miller also issued openly racist records. In 1964 he bought the former Ford dealership mapped here and put his studio upstairs; the building is now Crowley City Hall, with a museum of his equipment. His MasterTrak studio later hosted John Fogerty and Paul Simon.
listen_1_label: Interview with J.D. Miller, 1979 (Center for Louisiana Studies archive)

name: Richard's Club
writeup: Eddie Richard opened this wooden roadhouse on U.S. 190 in Lawtell in 1947. In the 1950s it booked touring rhythm and blues acts such as B.B. King, Big Joe Turner and Jimmy Reed. After Richard began hiring Clifton Chenier it became the best-known zydeco dance hall anywhere, nicknamed the Grand Ole Opry of zydeco. Boozoo Chavis recorded a comeback album there in 1989, and John Delafose suffered a fatal heart attack on its stage in 1994. Eddie's son Kermon ran it from 1979 until his death in 2004. It closed as Richard's in 2006, later reopened as Miller's Zydeco Hall of Fame, and burned in 2017.

name: Slim's Y-Ki-Ki
writeup: Arnold "Slim" Gradney and his wife Irene Pratt Gradney ran this dance hall on the highway north of Opelousas, one of the first clubs where zydeco took shape. The usual founding date is 1947, although license records suggest the Y-Ki-Ki name, a nod to Slim's interest in Hawaii, was adopted around 1960. Clifton Chenier, John Delafose, Rockin' Sidney, Beau Jocque and later Keith Frank filled the floor with dancers. The Gradneys' son Tony closed the club in 2016, citing rising band fees and unruly crowds. A local zydeco preservation society has since been working toward restoring the building.
sources: Acadiana Historical: Slim's Y-Ki-Ki, Zydeco's Highs and Lows in Opelousas <https://acadianahistorical.org/items/show/234> | The Independent (Lafayette): on the closing of Slim's Y-Ki-Ki <https://theind.com/articles/22530/> | St. Landry Now: Zydeco History Unfolds Downtown <https://www.stlandrynow.com/uncategorized/zydeco-history-unfolds-downtown/>

name: Shreveport Municipal Auditorium (Louisiana Hayride)
writeup: From April 1948 until 1960 the Art Deco Municipal Auditorium was home to the Louisiana Hayride, a Saturday night barn dance sent out over Shreveport's 50,000-watt station KWKH. The show earned the nickname "Cradle of the Stars" because so many performers rose from its stage to national fame: Hank Williams first, then Webb Pierce, Slim Whitman, Jim Reeves, Johnny Cash, Johnny Horton and, beginning in 1954, a young Elvis Presley, whose mix of country, gospel and rhythm and blues pointed toward rock and roll. The building, constructed between 1926 and 1929, was named a National Historic Landmark in 2008.
sources: 64 Parishes: Louisiana Hayride <https://64parishes.org/entry/louisiana-hayride> | Wikipedia: Shreveport Municipal Memorial Auditorium <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreveport_Municipal_Auditorium> | Visit Shreveport-Bossier: Five places where music history was made <https://www.visitshreveportbossier.org/blog/post/five-places-where-music-history-was-made-in-shreveport-bossier/>

name: La Poussière
writeup: La Poussière, French for "the dust," is a Cajun dance hall that the Patin family opened in Breaux Bridge in 1955. When the highway department took the original site for a right-of-way, the club moved across the road to the red brick building it occupies today. Lawrence Patin, who started managing it at eighteen, has kept it going for more than half a century. Long devoted to Cajun bands alone, it has recently added zydeco, and it remains one of the few old Louisiana dance halls still standing, with live music every weekend.
sources: Heart of Louisiana: La Poussiere <https://heartoflouisiana.com/la-poussiere/> | Country Roads Magazine: Let's Go Dancin', the evolution of Louisiana French music venues <https://countryroadsmagazine.com/art-and-culture/music/let-s-go-dancin-the-evolution-of-louisiana-french-music-venu/>

name: Floyd's Record Shop (Swallow and Jin Records)
writeup: Floyd Soileau began selling records in 1956 from a small room at radio station KVPI, where he hosted a Cajun music show, and by 1958 had launched two labels: Swallow for Cajun music and Jin for the rock-and-roll-flavored style later called swamp pop. Jin scored with Rod Bernard's "This Should Go On Forever," Joe Barry's "I'm a Fool to Care" and Tommy McLain's "Sweet Dreams," while Swallow's 1965 Balfa Brothers album helped spark the Cajun revival. The longtime East Main Street store closed in 2012; a smaller shop reopened in 2016 on South Chataignier Street, which is the point mapped here.
listen_1_label: Flat Town Music Company (official label site)
sources: Flat Town Music Company: Our History <https://flattownmusic.com/history/> | OffBeat Magazine: Floyd's Record Shop is back <https://offbeat.com/articles/floyds-record-shop-back> | Wikipedia: Floyd Soileau <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floyd_Soileau>

name: Fats Domino's House
writeup: Antoine "Fats" Domino was born in New Orleans in 1928 and grew up in the Lower Ninth Ward. After his piano-driven records made him a star of early rock and roll he chose to stay in the old neighborhood, and in 1960 he built a modern split-level home at Caffin Avenue and Marais Street, a few blocks from where he was raised. The house at 1208 Caffin Avenue became a neighborhood landmark. Domino was rescued from it by boat during the flooding that followed Hurricane Katrina in 2005. He died in 2017. The house is closed to the public, and its street now also carries his name.
sources: Explore Louisiana: Fats Domino's House <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/music/fats-dominos-house> | PBS American Masters: Fats Domino timeline <https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/fats-domino-timeline-of-dominos-life-hits-and-career-highlights/6252/> | Slate: Fats Domino, New Orleans rock legend, is dead (Jordan Hirsch, 2017) <https://slate.com/culture/2017/10/fats-domino-new-orleans-rock-legend-is-dead.html>

name: Preservation Hall
writeup: In the 1950s Larry Borenstein let older jazz musicians hold informal sessions in his art gallery at 726 St. Peter Street. In 1961 Allan and Sandra Jaffe took over and turned the worn early-1800s building into Preservation Hall, a plain room with benches, no bar and no air conditioning, devoted to traditional New Orleans jazz. Players such as Sweet Emma Barrett, George Lewis, Punch Miller, and Billie and De De Pierce found steady work and new audiences there. Under Jim Crow it was a rare place where integrated bands and audiences shared a room. The touring Preservation Hall Jazz Band grew out of it.
listen_1_label: Preservation Hall (official site)
sources: 64 Parishes: Preservation Hall <https://64parishes.org/entry/preservation-hall> | Preservation Hall: About <https://preservationhall.com/about>

name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival at the Fair Grounds
writeup: Jazz Fest began in April 1970 in Congo Square, then called Beauregard Square, where roughly 350 people heard Duke Ellington, Mahalia Jackson, Clifton Chenier, the Olympia Brass Band and Mardi Gras Indians. Founded by George Wein with Quint Davis and Allison Miner, it outgrew the park within two years and moved to the infield of the Fair Grounds Race Course for its third edition, April 28 to 30, 1972. It has stayed there since, growing into one of the largest festivals in the country and a yearly showcase for nearly every Louisiana style. Its foundation also supports radio station WWOZ.

name: Sea-Saint Studios
writeup: Allen Toussaint and his business partner Marshall Sehorn opened Sea-Saint in a plain building on Clematis Street in Gentilly in 1973, wanting a studio that could compete with Nashville and Muscle Shoals. Records made there include the Meters' Rejuvenation, Dr. John's Desitively Bonnaroo, LaBelle's number one hit "Lady Marmalade," the Wild Tchoupitoulas' album, and Paul McCartney and Wings' Venus and Mars. In the early 1990s DJ Jimi cut an early studio bounce record here. The studio took more than six feet of water in Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and never reopened; the building still stands.

name: Studio in the Country
writeup: Recording engineer William "Bleu" Evans built this studio on 26 acres of pine woods between Bogalusa and Varnado, about 70 miles from New Orleans. Clifton Chenier and his Red Hot Louisiana Band cut Bogalusa Boogie here, an album later added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry. Clarence "Gatemouth" Brown and the Neville Brothers (Fiyo on the Bayou) recorded here too, alongside national acts such as Kansas and Stevie Wonder. The studio is still working. Accounts date its start to 1972; its own site says it has been recording since 1973.

name: Festivals Acadiens et Créoles (Girard Park)
writeup: On March 26, 1974, more than eight thousand people filled Lafayette's Blackham Coliseum for A Tribute to Cajun Music, produced by Barry Ancelet and the staff of CODOFIL. There was deliberately no dance floor: the organizers wanted the crowd to sit and listen to Dennis McGee, Nathan Abshire, Marc Savoy, Clifton Chenier and Dewey Balfa. The night is remembered as a milestone for French Louisiana music. In 1976 the event moved outdoors to Girard Park, dancing was allowed, and it grew into a free festival now held each October. It was renamed Festivals Acadiens et Créoles in 2008 to recognize Creole musicians.

name: Maple Leaf Bar
writeup: The Maple Leaf opened on Oak Street in the Carrollton neighborhood on February 24, 1974, with Andrew Hall's Society Jazz Band, who then played every Saturday for seven years. It became one of the city's longest-running music clubs, with a band on its small stage seven nights a week. The pianist James Booker held forth here, and a set of his performances was later issued as Resurrection of the Bayou Maharajah. Rebirth Brass Band, another fixture, recorded the live album The Main Event here, and Walter "Wolfman" Washington, Henry Butler and Papa Grows Funk were regulars.

name: Tipitina's
writeup: In 1977 a group of young music fans turned the old 501 Club, a longshoremen's bar at Napoleon Avenue and Tchoupitoulas Street, into a stage for the pianist Henry Roeland Byrd, known as Professor Longhair. They named it for his 1953 song "Tipitina," and he played there until his death in 1980. The Meters, the Neville Brothers, Dr. John, the Radiators and Snooks Eaglin made it a home base, and in the early 1980s radio station WWOZ broadcast from upstairs. The club went bankrupt in 1984, reopened in 1986, and in 2018 was bought by members of the funk band Galactic.

name: Tabby's Blues Box and Heritage Hall
writeup: Bluesman Ernest "Tabby" Thomas opened this club in 1979 in a worn brick building, once a drugstore, at 1314 North Boulevard near the railroad tracks in Baton Rouge's old Black business district. It gave the city's swamp blues players a steady stage: Silas Hogan, Guitar Kelley, Henry Gray and Whispering Smith all performed there, and younger musicians including Kenny Neal, Tab Benoit and Thomas's son Chris Thomas King played its open jam sessions. The building was torn down in 1999 for a railroad overpass. Thomas reopened on Lafayette Street in 2000 and closed for good in 2004. Some accounts give 1978 as the opening year.

name: The Glass House
writeup: The Glass House was a windowless Central City bar about the size of a living room. From roughly 1980 to 1987 the Dirty Dozen Brass Band played there every Monday night, starting after eleven, for a dollar at the door with free red beans and rice. In that room the band worked out a new brass sound that drew on modern jazz and funk, dancers answered with new steps, and brass band music became a nightclub draw as well as a parade tradition. Rebirth Brass Band took over the residency and recorded a live album there in 1990. Black Masking Indians also held Sunday practices at the bar. The site is now an empty lot.

name: Natchitoches-NSU Folk Festival (Prather Coliseum)
writeup: Each July since 1980, Northwestern State University's Louisiana Folklife Center has filled Prather Coliseum with the state's traditional musicians and craftspeople. The festival was started to bring folk traditions to audiences in Louisiana and neighboring states, and its three stages put Cajun, zydeco, blues, bluegrass, gospel and country players on the same bill. It is also home to the Louisiana State Fiddle Championship. More than a hundred craftspeople demonstrate their work, and the program includes Cajun and zydeco dance lessons and talks with tradition bearers.

name: Southwest Louisiana Zydeco Music Festival (Plaisance)
writeup: In 1982, worried that zydeco and Creole music were dying out, Black Creole residents of the Opelousas area staged a festival on a farm field at Plaisance, north of town, with the backing of the Southern Development Foundation. Accounts credit a citizens' group called the Treasures of Opelousas and a committee from Holy Ghost Catholic Church led by the Rev. Albert McKnight. About four hundred people came the first year. The event grew into one of the country's leading zydeco festivals and the foundation's main fundraiser. In 2016 it left the Plaisance field, mapped here, for the indoor Yambilee grounds in Opelousas, where it has been held since.

name: Festival International de Louisiane
writeup: Festival International opened in downtown Lafayette on July 2, 1987, with a ceremony at city hall. Herman Mhire, director of the university art museum, was its founding president, and the city's community development director Phil Lank pushed it as a way to revive downtown during the oil bust. Its purpose is to celebrate the region's French heritage and its ties to the wider French-speaking world, so Cajun, Creole and zydeco bands share stages with performers from Canada, France, Haiti, Mali and elsewhere. It moved to late April in its second year, remains free, and now draws about 300,000 people.

name: Liberty Theatre and Rendez-vous des Cajuns
writeup: The Liberty opened in 1924 as a thousand-seat movie and vaudeville house and closed in 1982. Local volunteers restored it, and on July 11, 1987, it reopened with Rendez-vous des Cajuns, a Saturday night live show often likened to a Cajun Grand Ole Opry, developed with Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve. Folklorist Barry Jean Ancelet was emcee for twenty-four years and Ann Savoy booked the bands for the first fifteen, mixing Cajun groups, zydeco and Creole players and humorists. The show stopped in March 2020; a local association is restoring the building.

name: Ghost Town Lounge
writeup: Bounce, New Orleans's own form of hip-hop, is usually traced to this small bar in Hollygrove, in the 17th Ward. In 1991 MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv Phillips performed here over a loop from the Showboys' "Drag Rap," the beat locals call Triggerman, with Tucker calling out nearby neighborhoods and the crowd shouting back. A cassette of the routine, "Where Dey At," known as the red tape, is widely considered the first bounce release. The call-and-response chants and that beat became the template for DJ Jimi, Cash Money's early records and, later, Big Freedia. The building is no longer in use as a club.

name: Magnolia Projects (C.J. Peete) and Cash Money Records
writeup: The C.J. Peete public housing development, built in Central City in 1939 and known to everyone as the Magnolia, became the best-known address in New Orleans hip-hop. Brothers Bryan "Baby" Williams and Ronald "Slim" Williams started Cash Money Records around 1991 and tied the label to the complex. Juvenile and Turk of the Hot Boys grew up there, and Juvenile's 1998 video for "Ha" showed it to the country. Soulja Slim began rapping here as Magnolia Slim in 1993, and bounce artist Magnolia Shorty carried its name. The City Council voted in 2007 to demolish the complex; the mixed-income Harmony Oaks development now stands on the site.

name: Tunica-Biloxi Pow Wow
writeup: Each spring the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana hosts a Pow Wow on its reservation at Marksville. According to the chairman of the tribe's Pow Wow committee, the gathering in its present form dates to 1995; before that the tribe held a Green Corn festival every summer. Dancers and performers from many Native nations take part in inter-tribal dances and judged dance competitions, alongside traditional Tunica-Biloxi songs and dances, storytelling and Native flute. The tribe describes the event as a way to honor its ancestors, strengthen ties among its citizens and guests, and show visitors that Native people and their traditions are very much present.

name: Backstreet Cultural Museum
writeup: Sylvester Francis began filming second lines, jazz funerals and Carnival in Tremé around 1970. In 1999 he opened this museum in a former funeral home in the neighborhood to hold his photographs and films along with Mardi Gras Indian suits and objects from jazz funerals and second line parades. It works as much as a meeting place as a gallery: the Northside Skull and Bone Gang sets out from it on Mardi Gras morning, Indian gangs gather there, and the museum hosts an All Saints' Day procession meant to keep the jazz funeral alive. After Hurricane Ida damaged the original building in 2021, the museum moved in 2022 to St. Philip Street.
sources: 64 Parishes: Backstreet Cultural Museum <https://64parishes.org/?p=57024> | Wikipedia: Backstreet Cultural Museum <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backstreet_Cultural_Museum>

name: Delta Music Museum and Arcade Theater
writeup: Ferriday, a small town in Concordia Parish, produced three cousins who became famous in three different fields: rock and roll pianist Jerry Lee Lewis, country star Mickey Gilley and television evangelist Jimmy Swaggart. This museum on Louisiana Avenue, set up in 2001 by a local friends group and the state and run by the Louisiana Secretary of State's office, tells their story and honors some thirty blues, gospel, soul and country artists from the delta region. Exhibits also recall Haney's Big House, the Ferriday club on the chitlin' circuit that burned in 1966. The adjoining Arcade Theater hosts live performances.

name: Louisiana Swamp Pop Museum
writeup: Swamp pop is the rhythm-and-blues-flavored rock and roll that south Louisiana teenagers made their own in the late 1950s and early 1960s, trading the Cajun accordion and fiddle for electric guitars and horns. Ville Platte, where radio station KVPI pushed the new records, was proclaimed the Swamp Pop Capital of the World by the Louisiana Legislature, and in 2010 this museum opened in the town's old train depot. It displays stage costumes, photographs, records and a wall of autographs, and explains why so many performers took stage names, as Bobby Charles Guidry did for "See You Later, Alligator."
